source.name: NYC Business Glossary (NYC Small Business Services)

terms.def: A sworn, signed statement that some condition has been met. The signer is legally accountable if the statement later proves false and the condition was not met.

The kind of change in use or structure to an existing building that needs a DOB permit. There are three types, from more to less change: Alteration-1 (Alt-1), Alteration-2 (Alt-2) and Alteration-3 (Alt-3).

A change to a permit after it was first approved, which requires filing an amendment application. Changes often arise during construction as new information comes up and need a Post-Approval Amendment.
The power a building owner has, even without a permit, to make changes to the structure or use of a property.
A fiber in some building materials, such as insulation and roofing, that can cause health problems. Building owners must control it during renovations or other work by hiring special contractors.
The status in BISWeb of a plan or document that has been given to an individual agency employee to review.
A legal review to make sure a legal form was completed truthfully or work was performed correctly.
A cover over the sidewalk supported from the wall, not the ground. It needs a permit to install. See also Canopy.
A device that keeps contaminated water (such as water mixed with bleach) from flowing from a business back into the NYC drinking water supply.
A unique seven-digit number that the NYC Department of City Planning assigns to each building, used on DOB's BISWeb.
DOB's online database for any property in New York City, including violations, applications and inspections, and for registered contractors.
The uses and activities allowed in a building, as defined by the Certificate of Occupancy DOB issues for it.
The City agency that oversees construction and maintenance of buildings in New York City and the uses allowed in them.
Wages an employer must pay under State law when sending an employee home early for lack of work.
A cover over the sidewalk held up by poles fixed in the sidewalk. It requires a permit. See also Awning.

terms.term: Certificate of Appropriateness, Certificate of Minor Work, or Certificate of No Effect
terms.def: Formal approvals from the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission for work on a historic building. The glossary says one is needed when the work does not need a DOB permit, whether or not it affects architectural details.
A formal document linking the name customers see (the assumed or doing-business-as name) to the business's legal name on legal documents.
A document approving a business to collect sales tax on behalf of New York State.
A business zoning district mapped within residential districts so local retail such as grocery stores, dry cleaners and restaurants can locate near residents.
Any retail, service or office use, including all eating and drinking places, allowed as of right in areas listed by the Department of City Planning, or allowed by special permit.
A private, federally certified bank or credit union that aims to bring economic equality to underserved communities by lending to small and medium-size businesses.

A local representative body of 50 members, half nominated by City Council members and half by the Borough President. Boards oversee local government services and advise on land use and liquor license decisions.

The former name of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP): the City agency that licenses and regulates more than 78,000 businesses in 55 industries and enforces the Consumer Protection Law and other City, State and federal laws.

terms.term: Consumer and Worker Protection, NYC Department of
terms.def: The City agency, formerly the Department of Consumer Affairs (DCA), that licenses and regulates more than 78,000 businesses in 55 industries and enforces the Consumer Protection Law and other City, State and federal laws.

A professional who must be licensed to perform a specific role in getting permits, planning, building, opening or operating a business. Depending on the role, contractors are licensed by DOB (such as general contractors), DCWP (such as home improvement contractors) or another government body.
A change in a building's use, which DOB must formally recognize.
A practice at a food establishment that endangers public health and may lower the letter grade from a Health Department inspection. Some must be fixed before food can be served or a permit issued.
When harmful micro-organisms or substances move from one food to another, typically from raw food to ready-to-eat food.
Work that takes apart or tears down a structure, including part of an interior during a business remodel. DOB requires a work permit.

terms.term: Department of Consumer Affairs Adjudication Tribunal
terms.def: An administrative court that hears cases on violations of the City's licensing laws, the Consumer Protection Law and other laws enforced by DCWP.
An online hub that speeds approval of construction projects by letting architects and engineers submit digital construction plans to City agencies.
Wages that make up for lost pay due to permanent physical or mental impairment, as required by federal law.
The status of an application that is not approved at a given moment. Applications can usually be changed and resubmitted for approval without starting over.
The name customers see for a business, which may differ from its name on legal documents. See also Certificate of Assumed Name.
A tax form employees give their employer so the correct federal income tax is withheld from their pay.
A number used to identify and track a business for federal tax purposes, also called a Federal Tax Identification Number.
A form employers must complete for each new hire to prove the person is legally allowed to work in the United States.
A City court that handles quality-of-life violations, such as sanitation and noise, in New York City.
A non-criminal quality-of-life violation, such as a dirty sidewalk or lack of rodent control, issued by several City agencies and heard by the Environmental Control Board.
The City agency charged with protecting New York City's natural environment.
A hired third party who, for a fee, carries documents between an architect, engineer or contractor and City agencies.

terms.term: Financial Services, New York State Department of
terms.def: The State agency that regulates state-licensed and state-chartered financial institutions, and helps people and businesses understand financial products and make insurance and other claims.

The City agency responsible for fire safety citywide. It oversees fire risk and public safety rules, reviews construction plans and inspects businesses for issues like kitchens, exits and large gathering spaces.
An official drawing by a licensed professional of an existing or planned space seen from above, with technical details; sometimes called blueprints. See also Site Plans.

A certificate earned by completing the Health Department's course on safely preparing and serving food. A worker holding one must be present at all times while food is prepared or served at a food service establishment.
A place that serves food directly to customers, such as a restaurant, bakery, coffee shop or bar.
A practice at a food establishment that poses risks to public health and may lower the letter grade from a Health Department inspection.
A system that separates fats, oils and grease from wastewater to prevent sewer clogs. DEP requires them for food service establishments and some other businesses.
A sink used only for washing hands, required in every bathroom and within 25 clear feet of anywhere a worker prepares or serves food. See also Ware Washing Sinks.

terms.term: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point Plan
terms.def: A document that tracks food from arrival at an establishment until it is served, identifying food safety threats and ways to eliminate them. See also Potentially Hazardous Food.

terms.term: Health and Mental Hygiene, NYC Department of
terms.def: The City agency that oversees health and safety rules in New York City, including inspecting food service establishments and licensing various businesses.
Risk management that protects one or more people against health care costs. Most employees in New York can get it through their employers. See also Insurance.

An area of special architectural, historic and/or social value that the Landmarks Preservation Commission regulates to protect. Businesses in historic districts face special rules for renovating their buildings or spaces.
The temperature at which certain foods must be kept before cooking or serving, monitored according to Health Department guidelines. See also Potentially Hazardous Food.
The number in a street address identifying residential and commercial buildings, used in DOB's Building Information System and the same as the one the US Postal Service uses.
A sign plugged into electricity, such as a neon "Open" sign. DOB regulates these separately from other signs. See also Sign.

terms.term: Imminent Health Hazard (or Public Health Hazard) in Food Safety
terms.def: A practice at a food establishment that immediately threatens public health. If found during a Health Department inspection, it must be corrected before the restaurant can reopen or receive a grade.
An online tool that helps new or existing businesses find City, State and federal financial incentives they may be eligible for.
A drain pipe that does not connect directly to a drain but empties through an air gap into a drain or other plumbing, so waste below the gap cannot back up into the pipe above.
The set period, such as once a year, within which many businesses, buildings and license holders are checked for compliance. Cycles can vary, sometimes based on past inspection results.

Financial protection against loss: you pay a set amount each period and are paid for losses from unplanned events. Many types are required to own or lease space or employ workers, and proof of insurance is required for certain permits and licenses.
The federal agency that collects taxes from individuals and businesses.
The broad category of work in a DOB permit application, such as NB for New Building and Alt-1, Alt-2 and Alt-3 for alteration types.

terms.term: Labor, New York State Department of
terms.def: The State agency that oversees laws on worker safety and fair labor practices.
The federal agency that oversees laws on workers' rights, safety, health and income stability.
A building or site legally recognized for its historic value, regulated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission and requiring special permission to change.
The City agency that designates landmarks, historic districts and historic properties, and limits the changes businesses can make to them over time.
The legal approval of a space's owner for a business's use of that space.
A legal agreement between an owner (lessor) and a user (lessee) of a space, which helps define what activities are allowed there.
A grade card issued by the Health Department summarizing a restaurant's inspection results for customers. It must be displayed at all food service establishments; "A" is the highest grade.
A DOB letter equivalent to a Certificate of Occupancy for buildings built before 1938.
The legal responsibility of a party to repay debts it made, or that another party legally tied to it made. For example, a business partner may be liable to the business.
Permission from the State Liquor Authority for a business to serve alcohol. Different licenses apply to different business types, types of alcohol, and on-site or off-site consumption.
The least an employee must be paid per hour of work, set by City, State and federal law. See also Wages.
A DOB job type for permitting construction of entirely new structures or additions.
The City law regulating noise, including volume limits and times of day for activities such as music, construction and promotional events. Some violations go before the Environmental Control Board.
Floors, countertops, walls and ceilings not used for food preparation but still regulated by the Health Department because they indirectly affect food safety.
A copy of a document signed by all parties before a Notary Public, who authenticates it so it can be relied on in later legal processes.

A notice issued when a business fails to comply with a law enforced by the Department of Consumer Affairs (DCWP). It explains how to settle or appear before an Administrative Law Judge to present a defense.
A notice issued when a business fails to comply with a rule subject to the Environmental Control Board. It explains how to settle or appear before the ECB to contest the violation.
An online map showing City data by geography (a geographic information system, GIS), offered as part of NYC Open Data.

terms.term: Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings
terms.def: The City agency that hears and resolves challenges to violations issued by some City agencies, boards and commissions.

terms.term: Office of Child Support Enforcement Form
terms.def: A Human Resources Administration form for reporting child support responsibilities, which an individual must complete before applying for many NYC licenses and permits.
An online portal with information on common New York State licenses businesses need.
Time worked beyond 40 hours a week, for which State law requires an employee be paid an additional amount.
The step in a permit or license application where drawings are reviewed to confirm a space complies with rules. In DOB's BISWeb, "P/E" means an application is in Plan Examination.
A common class of DOB applications for changing a space's use or shape. For example, a PW-1 is needed for renovation and a PW-6 for a new Certificate of Occupancy.
Keeping ingredients in a refrigerator at the food preparation area so they stay as cold as needed throughout preparation.

Any food that can support growth of dangerous microorganisms, such as raw and cooked animal products (like meat and milk) and cooked starches (like potatoes and rice). A HACCP plan may be used to reduce risks.

terms.term: Power of Attorney / Authority to Act
terms.def: Legal permission, set out in a legal document, for one person to act on behalf of another, often to manage documents for them.

terms.term: Pre-Permit / Pre-Operational Health Inspections or Consultations
terms.def: A Health Department consultation for restaurants not yet open, confirming compliance with health laws. It carries no operating fines and helps a restaurant open faster. See also Inspection Cycle.
The part of a lease where the owner prohibits certain activities in the space, which may bar the tenant from things that would otherwise be legal.
A company that hauls waste for businesses.
A process letting a licensed architect or engineer self-approve projects without initial DOB review.
A person licensed by New York State to design or evaluate building spaces under applicable rules. PEs often work with registered architects and contractors.
A meeting before a government decision-making body where anyone can comment on a proposal.
An announcement the law requires, often in widely read newspapers, a set number of days before a public hearing or upcoming action.
An exhaust system for hot air required for large commercial stoves. Range hoods need special permits from the Fire Department.
A type of backflow prevention device reliable enough for restaurant kitchen uses, but not for bathroom or other high-hazard business uses, as required by law. See also Backflow Prevention Device.
A person licensed by New York State to design and submit drawings for construction and interior layouts.
Permission, obtained by application and fee, to use public space such as part of a sidewalk or park for a partly private use.
Cleaning an object or area to reduce harmful microorganisms to an acceptable level; a term often used in Health Department rules.
A formal document listing conditions or materials that must be approved or used for a project to proceed or a permit to be approved.
The City law regulating emission of pollutants and other harmful substances into the air.
A food preparation facility giving food retailers or preparers access to shared equipment. Operators must be permitted by the Health Department.
Outdoor business signs that are electric or above a certain size need DOB permits. BISWeb marks them "SG."
An official drawing showing a planned space and its surroundings, such as sidewalk, neighboring buildings, parking or street front. See also Floor Plans.
A business owned and run by one person, which files paperwork and taxes differently from other businesses.
The federal application for an Employer Identification Number, required for filing taxes. Sole proprietorships are exempt. See also Employer Identification Number.
The State agency that oversees the sale of alcoholic beverages in New York State.
A unique number for each block in New York City, used to track information about the block, such as taxes.
A unique number for each property in a block, used by the Department of Finance to track information about the property.

terms.term: Taxation and Finance, New York State Department of
terms.def: The State agency that oversees taxes and finance in New York State, including sales and property taxes.
An identifying number the IRS uses for tax purposes. See also Employer Identification Number.
The amount below minimum wage an employer may pay a waiter or other service worker for hours serving tipping customers, expected to be made up by tips so the worker still earns the full minimum wage.
A program all employers pay taxes into that provides income to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own. See also Insurance.
Money paid to a worker, regulated differently by City, State and federal governments.
A separate sink only for washing pots, pans and dishes, not hands or raw food. It must connect to special plumbing that captures grease before wastewater enters the sewer. See also Hand-Wash Sink.
The kind of work on a building, such as plumbing or electrical, that must be shown on DOB work permits.
A program that repays workers for damages and lost wages from work-related injuries. Generally, employers must provide it to all workers, with some exceptions.
The laws regulating the use and form of buildings and areas, set by the Department of City Planning and DOB. Zoning determines where specific types of businesses can locate.

rules.rule: Food Protection Certificate holder on site
rules.what: A worker holding a Health Department Food Protection Certificate must be present at all times while food is prepared or served at a food service establishment.
Every food service establishment must display its Health Department letter grade card.
A hand-wash-only sink is required in every bathroom and within 25 clear feet of any place a worker prepares or serves food.
Sinks for washing pots, pans and dishes must connect to special plumbing that captures grease before wastewater enters the sewer.
DEP requires grease interceptors (grease traps) for food service establishments and some other businesses.
An imminent health hazard found during a Health Department inspection must be corrected before the restaurant can reopen or receive a grade.
rules.penalty: Restaurant cannot reopen or be graded until corrected

rules.what: Some critical violations must be corrected before food can be served or a permit issued, and they may lower the letter grade.
Large commercial stoves require a range hood, which needs a special permit from the Fire Department.
Shared kitchen operators must be permitted by the Health Department.
Outdoor business signs that are electric or larger than a certain size require DOB permits.
Sidewalk awnings and canopies require a permit to install.
Any demolition, even part of an interior during a business remodel, requires a DOB work permit.
Building owners must control asbestos during renovations or other work by hiring special contractors.

Landmarks and buildings in historic districts require special permission from the Landmarks Preservation Commission to change; work that does not need a DOB permit needs a Certificate of Appropriateness, Minor Work or No Effect.
Under State law, employees must be paid an additional amount for time worked beyond 40 hours per week.
Under State law, employers must pay wages to an employee sent home early for lack of work.
Employees must be paid at least the minimum hourly wage set by City, State and federal law.
Employers must complete an Employment Eligibility Verification (I-9) for each person hired, proving they may legally work in the United States.
All employers must pay taxes into the unemployment insurance program.
Employers generally must provide workers' compensation insurance to all workers, with some exceptions.
Individuals must complete the Office of Child Support Enforcement form before applying for many NYC licenses and permits.
A business must have a State Liquor Authority license to serve alcohol.
A business must have a Certificate of Authority to collect sales tax on behalf of New York State.
